target_customer: Parents of children who suffer night terrors, buying a consumer device
problem: Night terrors disturb children and whole families. The known remedy, scheduled awakenings, requires parents to wake the child by hand before an episode.
business_model: Consumer hardware sold direct (under-mattress vibrating device with a phone app), with a planned suite of children's sleep products
product_category: Consumer sleep tech hardware for children

founders.name: Andy Rink
education: Stanford Biodesign Fellowship (per YC long description)
founders.background_notes: YC page describes him as a doctor and father, later a surgeon turned telehealth leader at Truepill. Employers before founding not stated in sources opened.

founders.name: Varun Boriah
founders.background_notes: YC long description calls him a medical device entrepreneur. YC page lists only later roles (Truepill, Alto Pharmacy, Luminai).

exit.reason: One database (CB Insights) says the product was not effective enough for the company to feel comfortable launching, so it wound down and returned money to investors. No company statement found.

technical_complexity.rationale: A small under-mattress vibration device with sensing, an app and a learning algorithm, plus the harder clinical task of showing it prevents night terrors. CBS reported in 2016 that the research was not yet published.

defensibility.rationale: The company called its technology patented and clinically proven, but independent efficacy data was not public and the scheduled awakening method it automates dates to the 1980s.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: No larger player was found building the same wedge in 2015. The product was reported out of production by March 2021.

market_need_then: Parents already tried scheduled awakenings by hand. The 2015 TechCrunch launch coverage and NPR coverage show parent interest, and 150 beta families tested the device.

branding.domain_note: Company site was lullysleep.com per a third party directory, not the plain lully.com.

identity.visual_style: Calm consumer product aimed at parents; no brand page was found
identity.voice_and_tone: Clinical and reassuring, with claims about clinically proven results

branding.community_and_virality: Covered by NPR, CBS, CNBC, TechCrunch and New Atlas in 2015 and 2016, mostly about the product. No fan community found.

brand_strength.rationale: Good press about the product, but no evidence of a lasting brand. An unrelated meditation app named Lully shares the name.

outcome_analysis: Lully raised a $2.1M seed in June 2015 and launched the Sleep Guardian and later the Sleep Guardian Plus in 2016. A single database says the product was not effective enough to launch confidently, so the company wound down and returned investor money. The device was reported out of production by March 2021. The shutdown date and the company's own reasons are not public, so the tech_unsolved factor rests on that one source.
notes: Company website was not fetched because the YC page lists none and a third party reports it returns a server error. TechCrunch March 2015 said $920k raised in total before YC graduation, and CB Insights and CNBC (via a secondary site) give about $2.2M total over 4 rounds, so earlier smaller rounds probably exist but are undated. The TechCrunch article did not name investors; the investor list comes from YC's company description and Bouncewatch, an aggregator. No dated competitor was found in a 2015 competitor search, so the list is empty.
